_about: Nerd facts for Rivers & oceans, Lakes & seas, Mountains, Deserts and Landmarks cards (the 🤓 Nerd facts pop-up). Keyed by card id. Each fact: [label, text], kid-friendly, 160 characters max.

amazon: The arapaima, one of the biggest freshwater fish on Earth, lives in the Amazon. It can grow about 10 feet long!
Pink river dolphins, called botos, swim through the Amazon's flooded forests.
Not a single bridge crosses the main Amazon River. People use boats and ferries instead.
nile: At about 4,130 miles, the Nile is often called the longest river in the world.
The White Nile and the Blue Nile meet in Khartoum, Sudan, to form the main Nile.
Every summer the Nile used to flood, leaving rich mud that helped ancient Egyptians grow wheat for bread.
yangtze: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze is the biggest power station in the world.
At about 3,900 miles, the Yangtze is the third-longest river on Earth.
Shanghai, one of the world's biggest cities, sits where the Yangtze meets the sea.
mississippi: Huge numbers of North America's ducks, geese and swans follow the Mississippi on their yearly migration.
Mud carried by the river built much of southern Louisiana, land called the Mississippi River Delta.
Water skiing was invented on Lake Pepin, a wide part of the Mississippi, by Ralph Samuelson in 1922.
yenisei: The Yenisei carries more water into the Arctic Ocean than any other river.
The Sayano-Shushenskaya Dam on the Yenisei is the biggest power plant in Russia.
Water from Lake Baikal flows out through the Angara River, which joins the Yenisei.
yellow: The Yellow River is called China's 'Mother River,' because early Chinese culture grew up along its banks.
At about 3,400 miles, it's China's second-longest river, after the Yangtze.
At Hukou Waterfall, the whole muddy river squeezes into a narrow gap and roars down, looking golden.
ob: Together with its branch the Irtysh, the Ob forms one of the longest river systems in Asia.
In the far north, the Ob stays frozen for about half the year.
Novosibirsk, Russia's third-biggest city, grew up where a railway bridge crossed the Ob.
parana: The Itaipu Dam, on the Paraná between Brazil and Paraguay, is one of the most powerful power plants on Earth.
Paraná comes from a Tupi word often translated as 'like the sea.'
Near Buenos Aires, the Paraná splits into a maze of islands and channels called the Paraná Delta.
congo-river: The Congo is the only major river that crosses the equator twice.
Kinshasa and Brazzaville, two capital cities, face each other across the Congo River.
Only the Amazon carries more water than the Congo.
mekong: In Vietnam's Mekong Delta, people buy fruit and vegetables at markets held right on boats.
The Mekong giant catfish can weigh as much as a grizzly bear.
In Thai and Lao, its name, Mae Nam Khong, is often translated as 'Mother of Waters.'
niger-river: In Mali, the Niger spreads into a huge inland delta of lakes and wetlands, home to millions of birds.
The Niger starts in Guinea's hills, only about 150 miles from the Atlantic Ocean, then flows away from it.
Timbuktu, a famous city of books and learning, grew up near the Niger's big bend.
murray: Old paddle steamers still carry visitors along the Murray, like they carried wool in the 1800s.
The Murray cod, Australia's biggest freshwater fish, lives in the Murray.
For much of its length, the Murray forms the border between New South Wales and Victoria.
danube: The Danube flows through four capital cities: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
Composer Johann Strauss II wrote 'The Blue Danube,' one of the most famous waltzes ever.
The Danube begins in Germany's Black Forest and flows east to the Black Sea.
volga: About 40% of Russia's people live in the land drained by the Volga.
The Volga flows into the Caspian Sea, the largest lake on Earth.
Giant sturgeon fish swim in the Volga. Some can live for more than 100 years!
ganges: The Ganges river dolphin is nearly blind and finds its way using sound.
With the Brahmaputra, the Ganges forms the world's largest river delta, in India and Bangladesh.
The Sundarbans mangrove forest at its mouth is home to Bengal tigers that swim between islands.
indus: The country of India takes its name from the Indus River.
The Indus begins in Tibet and flows through India and Pakistan to the Arabian Sea.
Mohenjo-daro, a city by the Indus, had planned streets and covered drains about 4,500 years ago.
rhine: The Rhine Falls in Switzerland is one of the most powerful waterfalls in Europe.
Along the Middle Rhine in Germany, dozens of castles sit on the hills above the river.
Rotterdam, near the Rhine's mouth, is the biggest port in Europe.
mackenzie: In winter, parts of the Mackenzie freeze so hard that trucks drive across it on ice roads.
The Mackenzie flows north into the Beaufort Sea, part of the Arctic Ocean.
It's named after Alexander Mackenzie, who paddled it all the way to the Arctic in 1789.
zambezi: Hippos and crocodiles live along the Zambezi, Africa's fourth-longest river.
Kariba Dam on the Zambezi made Lake Kariba, the world's biggest human-made lake by the water it holds.
The Zambezi flows east across Africa into the Indian Ocean in Mozambique.
colorado-river: Hoover Dam on the Colorado holds back Lake Mead, the biggest reservoir in the USA when it's full.
The Colorado gives water to about 40 million people in seven US states and Mexico.
Colorado means 'colored red' in Spanish, after the river's reddish mud.
euphrates: At about 1,700 miles, the Euphrates is the longest river in western Asia.
The Euphrates begins in the mountains of Türkiye and flows through Syria and Iraq.
Near Basra, the Euphrates and Tigris join to form the Shatt al-Arab, which flows into the Persian Gulf.
st-lawrence: White beluga whales live in the St. Lawrence all year round.
Montreal and Quebec City both sit on the St. Lawrence.
French explorer Jacques Cartier sailed up the St. Lawrence in 1535, reaching the village that became Montreal.
rio-grande: Rio Grande means 'big river' in Spanish. In Mexico it's called the Río Bravo.
The Rio Grande begins high in Colorado's San Juan Mountains.
In Texas, the river makes a giant curve that gives Big Bend National Park its name.
missouri-river: The Missouri's nickname is the Big Muddy, because it carries so much silt.
The Missouri begins in Montana, where three rivers meet: the Jefferson, the Madison and the Gallatin.
Three state capitals sit on the Missouri: Bismarck, Pierre and Jefferson City.
ohio-river: Ohio comes from a Seneca word meaning 'great river.'
Where they meet in Cairo, Illinois, the Ohio actually carries more water than the Mississippi.
Louisville, Kentucky, home of the famous Louisville Slugger baseball bat, sits on the Ohio River.
columbia-river: Every year, salmon swim from the Pacific Ocean up the Columbia to lay their eggs.
The Columbia River Gorge is famous for windsurfing and kiteboarding, thanks to its strong, steady winds.
It's named after the Columbia Rediviva, the ship of American captain Robert Gray, who sailed into it in 1792.
hudson-river: The Hudson has ocean tides that reach about 150 miles upriver, all the way to Troy, New York.
The Hudson starts at Lake Tear of the Clouds, a tiny pond high in New York's Adirondack Mountains.
In 1807, Robert Fulton's steamboat chugged up the Hudson from New York City to Albany.
potomac-river: Potomac comes from an Algonquian name often translated as 'trading place.'
At Great Falls, the Potomac tumbles over jagged rocks just upstream of Washington, D.C.
George Washington's home, Mount Vernon, looks out over the Potomac.
yukon-river: In the 1890s, thousands of people floated down the Yukon to search for gold in the Klondike.
Yukon comes from a Native word meaning 'great river.'
The Yukon Quest sled dog race follows the frozen river for much of its trail.
arkansas-river: Colorado's stretch of the Arkansas River is one of the most popular whitewater rafting spots in the USA.
The Royal Gorge Bridge in Colorado hangs about 950 feet above the Arkansas River.
At about 1,450 miles, it's one of the longest branches of the Mississippi.
thames: The Thames begins as a tiny trickle in the Cotswold hills, at a spot called Thames Head.
In London, the Thames rises and falls with the ocean tide by up to about 23 feet.
The Thames Barrier has giant steel gates that swing up to protect London from very high tides.
pacific-ocean: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about 36,000 feet deep, deeper than Everest is tall.
Explorer Ferdinand Magellan named it 'Pacific,' meaning peaceful, because its waters looked calm.
Most of the world's volcanoes sit around the edge of the Pacific, in a loop called the Ring of Fire.
atlantic-ocean: The Atlantic is the second-biggest ocean, covering about a fifth of Earth's surface.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a giant mountain range, runs down the middle of the Atlantic, almost all of it underwater.
The Gulf Stream, a warm ocean current, carries warm water across the Atlantic toward Europe.
indian-ocean: The Indian Ocean is the third-biggest ocean, after the Pacific and the Atlantic.
Madagascar, the fourth-biggest island on Earth, sits in the Indian Ocean.
The Maldives, a nation of coral islands in the Indian Ocean, is the flattest country on Earth.
arctic-ocean: There's no land at the North Pole. It sits on floating sea ice in the middle of the Arctic Ocean.
Narwhals, whales with a long spiral tusk, live in the Arctic Ocean.
In summer, the sun never sets over much of the Arctic Ocean.
southern-ocean: National Geographic began mapping the Southern Ocean as Earth's fifth ocean in 2021.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the strongest ocean current on Earth, flows all the way around Antarctica.
Tiny shrimp-like krill swarm in the Southern Ocean and feed whales, penguins and seals.
kilimanjaro: Kilimanjaro has glaciers on top, even though it's close to the equator.
No climbing ropes are needed. Hikers can walk all the way to its top, Uhuru Peak.
Kilimanjaro is made of three volcanic cones: Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira.
everest: In Nepal, Everest is called Sagarmatha. In Tibet, it's called Chomolungma.
Its English name honors George Everest, a British surveyor who mapped India.
Winds near the top of Everest can blow faster than 100 miles per hour.
k2: K2 got its name from a survey list: it was peak number 2 in the Karakoram range.
K2 is known as one of the hardest mountains in the world to climb.
K2 is the highest point of the Karakoram mountains.
denali: Denali means 'the high one' in the Koyukon Athabascan language.
From its base to its top, Denali rises about 18,000 feet, more than Everest rises from its base.
Denali National Park is home to grizzly bears, moose, caribou and wolves.
aconcagua: Aconcagua stands about 22,800 feet tall, the highest point in the Americas.
It's part of the Andes, close to Argentina's border with Chile.
Aconcagua is one of the Seven Summits, the highest peaks on each continent.
mont-blanc: Mont Blanc means 'white mountain' in French.
A road tunnel more than 7 miles long runs right under Mont Blanc, linking France and Italy.
A sweet chestnut-and-cream dessert called Mont Blanc is named after the mountain.
elbrus: Elbrus has two summits. The west peak is a little higher than the east peak.
Elbrus is in the Caucasus Mountains, near Russia's border with Georgia.
Cable cars and chairlifts carry skiers high up the snowy slopes of Elbrus.
matterhorn: Disneyland in California has a roller coaster mountain modeled after the Matterhorn.
Zermatt, the village at its foot, doesn't allow gas-powered cars. People ride electric taxis instead.
Edward Whymper's team first reached the top of the Matterhorn in 1865.
fuji: Mount Fuji last erupted in 1707, more than 300 years ago.
Most people climb Fuji in July and August, and many hike through the night to see sunrise from the top.
Artist Hokusai made a famous set of prints called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
kosciuszko: Explorer Paul Strzelecki named it in 1840 after Tadeusz Kościuszko, a Polish hero.
Kosciuszko is one of the easiest of the Seven Summits. A walking path leads to its top.
Mount Kosciuszko is about 7,310 feet tall.
rainier: Rainier has more glaciers than any other mountain in the lower 48 states.
In summer, the meadows on Rainier's slopes burst with colorful wildflowers.
At 14,410 feet, Rainier is the highest mountain in Washington State.
olympus: At about 9,570 feet, Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece.
In the myths, Zeus, king of the gods, ruled from the top of Olympus.
The Olympus area became Greece's first national park in 1938.
table-mountain: When clouds pour over its flat top, locals say the 'tablecloth' is on.
A cable car with a spinning floor carries visitors to the top.
Table Mountain's rocks are hundreds of millions of years old, older than the Himalayas.
mount-kenya: The country of Kenya is named after Mount Kenya.
Mount Kenya sits just south of the equator, but it still has glaciers.
Mount Kenya is about 17,057 feet tall.
ararat: Ararat has two volcanic peaks, called Greater Ararat and Little Ararat.
At about 16,854 feet, Ararat is the highest mountain in Türkiye.
Ararat towers over Yerevan, Armenia's capital, and appears on Armenia's coat of arms.
etna: Etna is the tallest active volcano in Europe.
Etna's rich volcanic soil helps grow oranges, lemons and famous Bronte pistachios.
In winter, people can ski on Etna's snowy slopes.
mauna-kea: Mauna Kea's top has some of the world's biggest telescopes for studying stars.
Mauna Kea gets snow in winter, and its name means 'white mountain' in Hawaiian.
Measured from sea level, Mauna Kea is about 13,800 feet tall.
himalayas: The Himalayas are some of the youngest mountains on Earth, only about 50 million years old.
The Himalayan region holds so much ice that scientists call it the 'Third Pole.'
Shaggy yaks carry loads and give milk for butter and cheese in Himalayan villages.
andes: Potatoes were first grown as food in the Andes, thousands of years ago.
Llamas and alpacas come from the Andes. Alpaca wool is super soft and warm.
The Andes run through seven countries, from Venezuela down to Chile and Argentina.
rockies: Rain on one side of the Rockies' Continental Divide flows to the Pacific. On the other side, it heads to the Atlantic.
Mount Elbert in Colorado is the highest peak in the Rockies, at 14,440 feet.
Yellowstone, Glacier and Banff national parks are all in the Rocky Mountains.
alps: Famous cheeses like Gruyère and Emmental come from dairy farms in the Alps.
The first Winter Olympics were held in Chamonix, in the French Alps, in 1924.
Great rivers like the Rhine and the Rhône start in the Alps.
atlas-mountains: Toubkal in Morocco is the highest peak in the Atlas Mountains, at about 13,670 feet.
The High Atlas often gets snow, and Morocco has a ski resort there called Oukaïmeden.
Barbary macaque monkeys live in the forests of the Atlas Mountains.
urals: The Urals stretch about 1,500 miles, from the Arctic down to Kazakhstan.
The Urals are famous for gems like emeralds and alexandrite, a stone that changes color in different light.
The Urals are hundreds of millions of years old, so wind and rain have worn them low and rounded.
appalachians: The Appalachian Trail runs about 2,200 miles through the mountains, from Georgia to Maine.
Mount Mitchell in North Carolina is the highest peak in the Appalachians, at 6,684 feet.
Great Smoky Mountains National Park is the most-visited national park in the USA.
gobi: At sunset, the Gobi's Flaming Cliffs glow bright red and orange.
Wild Bactrian camels, with two humps, live in the Gobi.
Most of the Gobi is bare rock and gravel, not sand dunes.
sahara: In Libya's Sahara, the Ubari Lakes sit among giant dunes, fed by water from deep underground.
Date palms grow at oases, where water from underground reaches the surface.
Emi Koussi, a volcano in Chad, is the highest point in the Sahara.
arabian: The Arabian oryx, a white antelope, gets most of its water from the plants it eats.
Some dunes in the Arabian Desert make a deep booming hum when sand slides down them.
The Arabian Desert covers most of the Arabian Peninsula, about 900,000 square miles.
kalahari: Meerkats live in the Kalahari and take turns standing guard for their family.
Wild tsamma melons grow in the Kalahari and give animals and people water to drink.
The Kalahari covers much of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa.
namib: Sossusvlei in the Namib has some of the tallest sand dunes on Earth, glowing orange-red.
Some Namib beetles drink by catching fog droplets on their backs.
Namib means 'vast place' in the Nama language.
great-victoria: The Great Victoria Desert is about 134,000 square miles, bigger than the state of New Mexico.
The thorny devil lizard lives here and drinks water through tiny grooves in its skin.
Explorer Ernest Giles named it after Queen Victoria in 1875.
great-sandy: Long red sand dunes run in straight lines across the Great Sandy Desert.
Wolfe Creek Crater, made by a falling meteorite, sits at the desert's edge.
It's Australia's second-biggest desert, after the Great Victoria.
atacama: NASA has tested Mars rovers in the Atacama, because its ground is so much like Mars.
Its clear, dry skies make it one of the best places on Earth for telescopes, like ALMA.
In rare rainy years, the Atacama bursts into a carpet of flowers called the desierto florido.
mojave: Joshua trees, with their spiky arms, grow mainly in the Mojave.
Las Vegas is the biggest city in the Mojave.
Badwater Basin, in the Mojave's Death Valley, is the lowest point in North America, 282 feet below sea level.
sonoran: A saguaro cactus can grow more than 40 feet tall and live over 150 years.
The Sonoran gets rain in both winter and summer, making it one of the greenest deserts.
Phoenix and Tucson are both in the Sonoran Desert.
chihuahuan: The Chihuahuan Desert has more kinds of cactus than almost anywhere else on Earth.
White Sands National Park's glittering dunes are made of gypsum, not regular sand.
Carlsbad Caverns, with its giant underground rooms, lies beneath the Chihuahuan Desert.
taklamakan: Silk Road traders went around the Taklamakan's edges, stopping at oasis towns like Kashgar.
Most of the Taklamakan's sand dunes slowly move with the wind.
A highway crosses the desert, lined with plants watered by drip hoses to hold back the sand.
thar: The Pushkar Camel Fair, on the edge of the Thar, brings together thousands of camels each year.
Jaisalmer, the 'Golden City,' has a sandstone fort that glows yellow in the Thar.
The Thar is one of the most crowded deserts on Earth, with many villages and towns.
syrian: Bedouin people have herded camels, sheep and goats across this desert for hundreds of years.
Most of the Syrian Desert is flat, stony ground, not sand dunes.
Parts of it are covered with dark volcanic rocks, called the Harrat al-Sham.
patagonian: The Andes block rain clouds from the Pacific, keeping the Patagonian Desert dry.
Guanacos, wild relatives of the llama, roam the Patagonian Desert.
Magellanic penguins nest on its Atlantic coast, at a place called Punta Tombo.
karakum: In the Karakum, a giant crater called Darvaza has glowed with burning gas for decades.
Karakum means 'black sand' in Turkic languages.
The Karakum Canal, one of the longest canals on Earth, carries river water across the desert.
kyzylkum: Muruntau, one of the world's biggest gold mines, is in the Kyzylkum.
The Kyzylkum lies between two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya.
Steppe tortoises dig burrows in the Kyzylkum's sandy ground.
great-basin: Great Basin bristlecone pines are some of the oldest trees on Earth, nearly 5,000 years old.
Much of its rain falls as snow, which makes it a 'cold desert.'
Rivers in the Great Basin never reach the ocean. They end in lakes or soak into the ground.
danakil: At Dallol, bright yellow, green and orange hot springs make the ground look like another planet.
Camel caravans still carry blocks of salt out of the Danakil.
The Erta Ale volcano has a bubbling lake of lava.
lake-superior: Lake Superior's beaches are famous for agates, striped stones that shine when wet.
Storms on Lake Superior can whip up waves more than 25 feet tall.
In Duluth, Minnesota, a whole section of road on the Aerial Lift Bridge rises to let ships pass.
lake-michigan: Sleeping Bear Dunes rise about 450 feet above Lake Michigan.
Michigan has more lighthouses than any other state, many of them along Lake Michigan.
Traverse City, near the lake, calls itself the Cherry Capital of the World.
lake-huron: Manitoulin Island has its own lakes, including Lake Manitou, the biggest lake on an island in a lake.
Lake Huron is the second-biggest Great Lake by area, after Lake Superior.
The Blue Water Bridge links Michigan and Ontario where Lake Huron flows into the St. Clair River.
lake-erie: Lake Erie holds the least water of all the Great Lakes.
Cleveland, Toledo, Erie and Buffalo all sit on Lake Erie's shore.
Point Pelee, the southern tip of mainland Canada, pokes out into Lake Erie.
lake-ontario: Lake Ontario almost never freezes all the way across, because it's so deep.
Rochester, New York, near the lake, holds a big lilac festival every spring.
Sandbanks Provincial Park, on its Canadian shore, has some of the biggest freshwater sand dunes around.
great-salt-lake: Tiny brine shrimp live in the lake, and millions of birds stop by to eat them.
Part of the lake turns pink, thanks to tiny salt-loving microbes.
It's the largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere.
lake-tahoe: At about 1,645 feet deep, Tahoe is the second-deepest lake in the USA.
The border between California and Nevada runs right through the lake.
The 1960 Winter Olympics were held near Lake Tahoe, at the resort now called Palisades Tahoe.
crater-lake: No rivers flow into Crater Lake. It's filled only by rain and snow.
A small volcano called Wizard Island pokes up out of the lake.
A log called the Old Man of the Lake has floated upright in Crater Lake for more than 100 years.
lake-okeechobee: Lake Okeechobee is huge but shallow, only about 9 feet deep on average.
Water flowing south from the lake helps feed the Everglades.
Lake Okeechobee is famous for largemouth bass fishing.
lake-champlain: For a few weeks in 1998, Congress called Lake Champlain a sixth Great Lake.
Ferries carry cars across the lake between Vermont and New York.
It's named after French explorer Samuel de Champlain, who reached it in 1609.
great-bear-lake: Great Bear Lake and its land became a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2016.
Record-size lake trout, over 70 pounds, have been caught in Great Bear Lake.
The Arctic Circle runs across the northern part of the lake.
lake-winnipeg: Lake Winnipeg is one of the biggest freshwater lakes in the world, even bigger than Lake Ontario.
Fishers catch pickerel and whitefish in Lake Winnipeg.
Grand Beach, on its eastern shore, has soft white sand and tall dunes.
lake-titicaca: Titicaca is often called the highest lake that big boats can sail on, about 12,500 feet up.
The Titicaca water frog has baggy, wrinkly skin that helps it breathe in the chilly water.
In Inca stories, the first Inca rulers rose up out of Lake Titicaca.
lake-nicaragua: Bull sharks can swim up a river from the sea into Lake Nicaragua.
The colorful old city of Granada sits on the lake's shore.
People also call it Cocibolca, often translated as 'sweet sea.'
lake-baikal: Baikal is about 25 million years old, the oldest lake on Earth.
Nerpa seals live only in Lake Baikal, far from any ocean.
In winter, Baikal's ice can be so clear that you can see deep into the water below.
caspian-sea: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan all touch the Caspian Sea.
The Caspian's surface sits about 90 feet below sea level.
The Caspian seal, one of the smallest seals in the world, lives only here.
dead-sea: The Dead Sea is about 10 times saltier than the ocean.
Visitors cover themselves in its dark, mineral-rich mud.
The Dead Sea's water level drops about 3 feet every year.
lake-victoria: It's the second-biggest freshwater lake on Earth by area, after Lake Superior.
The equator runs right across the northern part of Lake Victoria.
British explorer John Speke named it after Queen Victoria in 1858.
lake-tanganyika: Lake Tanganyika is the second-deepest lake on Earth, after Lake Baikal.
It's one of the oldest lakes on Earth, millions of years old.
Gombe Stream, where Jane Goodall studied chimpanzees, is on the lake's shore.
lake-malawi: Lake Malawi is called the 'Lake of Stars,' after the twinkling lanterns of fishing boats at night.
Lake Malawi is about 360 miles long.
Malawi, Mozambique and Tanzania share the lake.
lake-chad: Lake Chad is much smaller than it was in the 1960s, because of less rain and more people using its water.
Chad, Cameroon, Niger and Nigeria all touch Lake Chad.
Kuri cattle have big puffy horns that help them float as they swim between the lake's islands.
lake-turkana: Central Island, in the lake, has one of the biggest groups of Nile crocodiles in the world.
Scientists have found some of the oldest fossils of early humans near Lake Turkana.
No river flows out of Lake Turkana. Water leaves only when it dries up in the heat.
lake-tana: Old monasteries on the lake's islands hold beautifully painted churches.
Fishers paddle boats called tankwas, made from papyrus reeds.
Lake Tana is the biggest lake in Ethiopia.
lake-volta: The Akosombo Dam, which made the lake, makes much of Ghana's electricity.
Lake Volta covers more than 3% of Ghana.
Old tree trunks still poke up out of the water where a forest was flooded.
lake-geneva: Lake Geneva is shaped like a crescent moon.
Movie star Charlie Chaplin lived near the lake, and a statue of him stands in Vevey.
In French, it's called Lac Léman.
lake-como: The town of Como has been famous for making silk for hundreds of years.
Lake Como is one of the deepest lakes in Europe, more than 1,300 feet deep.
The village of Bellagio, nicknamed the 'pearl of the lake,' sits where its arms meet.
loch-ness: Loch Ness is about 750 feet deep.
Loch Ness is part of the Caledonian Canal, which links Scotland's east and west coasts.
The ruins of Urquhart Castle sit on the loch's shore.
lake-ladoga: Valaam Island, in the lake, has a famous old monastery.
Lake Ladoga's water flows out through the Neva River and right through St. Petersburg.
A kind of ringed seal lives in Lake Ladoga, far from the sea.
lake-balaton: Balaton is shallow, so it warms up quickly for summer swimming.
The Tihany Peninsula pokes into the lake and is famous for lavender fields.
Lake Balaton is about 48 miles long.
issyk-kul: Issyk-Kul is one of the biggest mountain lakes on Earth, second only to Lake Titicaca.
Its water is slightly salty, which helps keep it from freezing.
It's Kyrgyzstan's favorite beach spot, ringed by the Tian Shan mountains.
lake-eyre: Lake Eyre is the lowest natural point in Australia, about 50 feet below sea level.
When it's dry, Lake Eyre is a huge, shiny white crust of salt.
Donald Campbell set a land speed record on its salt in 1964.
lake-taupo: Lake Taupō is famous for trout fishing.
Pumice from old eruptions is so light that it floats on the lake.
A Māori rock carving at Mine Bay is about 46 feet tall.
lake-vanern: Vänern is the third-largest lake in Europe.
The Göta Canal links Lake Vänern toward the Baltic Sea.
sea-of-galilee: Its Hebrew name, Kinneret, may come from kinnor, meaning harp, after the lake's shape.
The Sea of Galilee is Israel's biggest freshwater lake.
The Jordan River flows into the lake from the north and out again to the south.
mediterranean-sea: Mediterranean means 'in the middle of the land' in Latin.
It connects to the Atlantic through the Strait of Gibraltar, only about 8 miles wide.
Sicily is the biggest island in the Mediterranean.
caribbean-sea: The Caribbean is named after the Carib people, who lived on its islands.
Its deepest spot, in the Cayman Trough, is more than 25,000 feet deep.
The Mesoamerican Reef, off Mexico, Belize, Guatemala and Honduras, is the biggest reef in the Western Hemisphere.
red-sea: One idea is that the Red Sea is named after red algae that sometimes bloom on its surface.
No rivers flow into it, so the Red Sea is one of the saltiest seas in the world.
The Suez Canal links the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, so ships don't have to sail around Africa.
black-sea: Deep down, the Black Sea has almost no oxygen, so only tiny microbes live there.
Six countries touch it: Türkiye, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia and Georgia.
Three kinds of dolphins and porpoises live in the Black Sea.
baltic-sea: Golden amber, made from ancient tree sap, washes up on Baltic beaches.
The Baltic formed after the last Ice Age, about 10,000 years ago.
Nine countries line the shores of the Baltic Sea.
north-sea: Long ago, land now under the North Sea linked Britain to mainland Europe.
Gray and harbor seals rest on sandbanks in the Wadden Sea, part of the North Sea.
The Netherlands built giant dams and dikes to hold back the North Sea.
arabian-sea: For thousands of years, sailors crossed the Arabian Sea on monsoon winds to trade spices.
Mumbai and Karachi are big port cities on the Arabian Sea.
Lakshadweep is a group of coral islands in the Arabian Sea.
south-china-sea: Hundreds of tiny islands, reefs and sandbars dot the South China Sea.
It covers about 1.4 million square miles.
It washes the shores of Borneo, the third-biggest island on Earth.
bering-sea: During the Ice Age, a land bridge here linked Asia and North America.
Walruses and fur seals gather on the Bering Sea's islands.
It's named after Vitus Bering, a Danish explorer who sailed for Russia.
sea-of-japan: Fishing boats use bright lights at night to catch squid.
Cold winds over this sea bring heavy snow to Japan's west coast.
A warm current called the Tsushima Current flows into it from the south.
coral-sea: Parts of the Coral Sea are about 30,000 feet deep.
The tiny Coral Sea Islands belong to Australia.
Green sea turtles nest on the Coral Sea's islands.
tasman-sea: Australians and New Zealanders jokingly call the Tasman Sea 'the Ditch.'
In 1928, Charles Kingsford Smith made the first flight across the Tasman Sea.
Lord Howe Island, in the Tasman Sea, has the world's southernmost coral reef.
sargasso-sea: Floating golden sargassum seaweed covers the Sargasso Sea in patches.
European and American eels travel to the Sargasso Sea to lay their eggs.
Its water is some of the clearest in the whole ocean.
yellow-sea: Huge mudflats along the Yellow Sea are a stopping point for millions of migrating birds.
Tides at Incheon, Korea, can rise and fall by about 30 feet.
The Yellow Sea is shallow, mostly less than 300 feet deep.
eiffel-tower: A restaurant called Le Jules Verne sits on the Eiffel Tower's second floor.
Giant Olympic rings hung on the Eiffel Tower for the Paris 2024 Olympics.
Gustave Eiffel had the names of 72 French scientists and engineers engraved around the tower.
statue-of-liberty: The Statue of Liberty's index finger is 8 feet long.
Her crown has seven spikes and 25 windows.
Her tablet shows July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals.
golden-gate-bridge: It was the longest suspension bridge in the world when it opened in 1937.
San Francisco's famous fog even has a nickname: Karl.
Its two main cables hold about 80,000 miles of wire, enough to wrap around Earth three times.
great-wall: Despite the legend, the Great Wall is very hard to see from space with just your eyes.
Builders mixed sticky rice into the mortar to make some parts super strong.
Counting all its branches, the Great Wall is about 13,000 miles long.
taj-mahal: The Taj Mahal's walls are decorated with colorful stone flowers set into the marble.
About 20,000 workers built the Taj Mahal over about 20 years.
The Taj Mahal is almost perfectly symmetrical, the same on the left and the right.
colosseum: Under the arena floor, ancient elevators lifted scenery up into the show.
The Colosseum's real name was the Flavian Amphitheatre.
Italy's 5-cent euro coin shows the Colosseum.
machu-picchu: Llamas munch grass on Machu Picchu's terraces.
Explorer Hiram Bingham brought Machu Picchu to the world's attention in 1911.
Machu Picchu was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.
christ-the-redeemer: The statue was finished in 1931. It's made of concrete covered with small soapstone tiles.
Lightning strikes the statue a few times every year.
Its arms stretch about 92 feet from fingertip to fingertip.
pyramids-of-giza: The Great Sphinx, with a lion's body and a human head, sits beside the pyramids.
The pyramids were once covered in smooth white limestone that shone in the sun.
The Great Pyramid is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
sydney-opera-house: Danish architect Jørn Utzon designed the Sydney Opera House.
Its roof shells are all cut from the shape of one giant ball, like slices of an orange peel.
During the Vivid Sydney festival, colorful light shows are projected onto its roof.
big-ben: The tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
Each of the tower's four clock faces is about 23 feet across.
Clockkeepers add or remove old pennies on the pendulum to keep the clock on time.
mount-rushmore: The faces are George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln.
Gutzon Borglum led the carving from 1927 to 1941.
A Hall of Records room is hidden in the rock behind Lincoln's head.
petra: Petra's most famous building, the Treasury, appeared in an Indiana Jones movie.
The Nabataean people who built Petra collected rainwater with clever channels and pools.
Visitors walk into Petra through the Siq, a narrow canyon about three-quarters of a mile long.
chichen-itza: Clap your hands in front of the big pyramid, and the echo sounds like a bird chirping.
The big pyramid has 365 steps, one for each day of the year.
Chichén Itzá has a giant ball court where players hit a rubber ball with their hips.
stonehenge: Some of Stonehenge's smaller stones came from Wales, about 150 miles away.
Its biggest stones weigh about 25 tons, as much as four elephants.
Stonehenge's name probably comes from Old English words meaning 'hanging stones.'
leaning-tower-of-pisa: The Leaning Tower is the bell tower of Pisa's cathedral, and it has seven bells.
Engineers carefully straightened it a little between 1990 and 2001, so it won't topple.
A famous story says Galileo dropped balls from the tower to test how fast things fall.
angkor-wat: Crowds gather before dawn to watch the sun rise behind Angkor Wat's towers.
A moat about 600 feet wide surrounds the temple.
Its walls are carved with more than 1,500 graceful dancers and goddesses.
burj-khalifa: The Dubai Fountain at its base shoots water up to 500 feet into the air.
Its elevators zoom up at about 22 miles per hour.
Its shape was inspired by a desert flower called the spider lily.
sagrada-familia: In 2026, its giant Tower of Jesus Christ made the Sagrada Família the tallest church in the world.
Its columns branch out like trees, so the inside feels like a stone forest.
Antoni Gaudí worked on the Sagrada Família for more than 40 years.
parthenon: The Parthenon's columns bulge a tiny bit in the middle, so they look perfectly straight from far away.
A giant statue of Athena, covered in gold and ivory, once stood inside.
It's made of white marble from nearby Mount Pentelicus.
neuschwanstein: King Ludwig II of Bavaria built Neuschwanstein as his dream castle.
For its time it was high-tech, with running water, central heating and even a telephone line.
About 1.4 million people visit the castle each year.
saint-basils: Saint Basil's is really nine chapels joined together.
Saint Basil's Cathedral was built in the 1550s.
Today Saint Basil's is part of Russia's State Historical Museum.
forbidden-city: Its roofs are golden yellow, a color once kept just for the emperor.
Today it's the Palace Museum, one of the most visited museums on Earth.
Rows of little animal statues stand on the edges of its roofs.
tokyo-skytree: At night it's lit in two styles, a sky-blue one called Iki and a purple one called Miyabi.
Its height, 634 meters, can be read as 'Mu-sa-shi,' the old name of the Tokyo area.
hollywood-sign: The sign was first put up to advertise new homes.
In 1978, donors each paid for one new letter to rebuild the worn-out sign.
The original sign had about 4,000 light bulbs.
space-needle: The Space Needle is 605 feet tall.
Its elevators zip to the top in about 41 seconds.
It was built to stand up to winds of about 200 miles per hour.
gateway-arch: The Gateway Arch is covered in shiny stainless steel.
Visitors ride to the top in little egg-shaped tram pods that hold five people each.
It honors St. Louis as the 'Gateway to the West' for pioneers heading west.
niagara-falls: Niagara is really three waterfalls: Horseshoe Falls, American Falls and Bridal Veil Falls.
Maid of the Mist boats have carried visitors close to the falls since 1846.
Over about 12,000 years, rushing water has worn the falls about 7 miles upstream.
grand-canyon: The Grand Canyon is about 277 miles long.
Rocks at the canyon's bottom are nearly 2 billion years old.
The glass Skywalk lets visitors look straight down into the canyon.
brandenburg-gate: The Brandenburg Gate has 12 columns that form five passageways.
The Brandenburg Gate was finished in 1791.
The Brandenburg Gate appears on German euro coins.
tower-bridge: Many people mix up Tower Bridge with London Bridge, a plainer bridge nearby.
Tower Bridge's high walkways have glass floors.
edinburgh-castle: The Honours of Scotland, Scotland's crown jewels, are kept in Edinburgh Castle.
St. Margaret's Chapel, from the 1100s, is the oldest building in Edinburgh.
Edinburgh Castle is one of Scotland's most visited attractions.
moai: Some moai wear red stone hats called pukao.
Many moai aren't just heads. They have bodies hidden underground!
Legends say the moai 'walked.' Scientists think people rocked them upright along with ropes.
uluru: Uluru is a sacred place for the Anangu, the Aboriginal people of the area.
Like an iceberg, much of Uluru is thought to lie hidden underground.
Uluru rises about 1,142 feet above the flat land around it.
great-barrier-reef: The Great Barrier Reef stretches more than 1,400 miles.
It was built by tiny animals called coral polyps.
Six of the world's seven kinds of sea turtles live on the reef.
victoria-falls: Victoria Falls is more than a mile wide.
Its mist often fills with rainbows, and on bright full-moon nights, 'moonbows.'
A bridge built in 1905 crosses the gorge near the falls between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
hagia-sophia: Shiny gold mosaics glitter on Hagia Sophia's walls.
Its main dome is more than 100 feet across.
A friendly cat named Gli lived in Hagia Sophia for years and became world-famous.
golden-temple: The Golden Temple's upper floors are covered in real gold.
The temple stands in the middle of a pool called the Amrit Sarovar.
It has four entrances, to welcome people from every direction.
petronas-towers: The towers' floor plan is based on an eight-pointed star.
They're still the tallest twin towers in the world.
marina-bay-sands: Three hotel towers hold up the rooftop SkyPark, like a giant surfboard.
A nightly light-and-water show called Spectra dazzles Marina Bay.
The ArtScience Museum next door is shaped like a lotus flower.
iguazu-falls: Iguazu Falls is much wider than Niagara Falls.
Iguazu means 'big water' in the Guaraní language.
Coatis, long-nosed cousins of raccoons, roam the trails around the falls.
teotihuacan: Teotihuacan also has a Pyramid of the Moon at one end of its long main avenue.
Around the year 500, Teotihuacan was one of the biggest cities on Earth, with about 100,000 people.
Hot-air balloons float over the pyramids at sunrise.
mont-saint-michel: A golden statue of Saint Michael stands on top of the island's abbey.
The tides here are some of the biggest in Europe, and they rush in fast.
Mont-Saint-Michel is famous for giant fluffy omelets from La Mère Poulard.
alhambra: Alhambra means 'the red one' in Arabic, after its reddish walls.
The Court of the Lions has a fountain held up by 12 stone lions.
The Alhambra's tile patterns inspired the artist M.C. Escher.
cn-tower: The CN Tower is about 1,815 feet tall.
Its glass-front elevators zoom up to the LookOut level in under a minute.
Lightning strikes the CN Tower about 75 times a year.
empire-state-building: King Kong climbed the Empire State Building in the 1933 movie.
It has 1,576 steps from the lobby to the 86th floor.
The Empire State Building has its own zip code: 10118.
white-house: It takes about 570 gallons of paint to cover the outside of the White House.
The White House has a bowling lane and a movie theater.
Theodore Roosevelt made the name 'White House' official in 1901.
potala-palace: The Potala Palace has two parts: the White Palace and the Red Palace.
The Potala Palace is 13 stories tall.
The Potala Palace is pictured on China's 50-yuan banknote.
terracotta-army: Farmers digging a well found the Terracotta Army in 1974.
Clay horses and chariots stand with the figures.
The figures were once painted in bright colors.
old-faithful: Old Faithful's eruptions shoot about 100 to 180 feet high.
Yellowstone was the world's first national park, created in 1872.
Rangers predict Old Faithful's next eruption, usually to within about 10 minutes.
